body.heading: The one job of the host
paragraphs: A potluck is the friendliest kind of gathering: nobody cooks everything, nobody pays for everything, and everyone brings a piece of themselves to the table. Your job as host is not to control the menu — it is to make sure the table works. That means one main dish, a balance of the rest, and no awkward duplicates.

The simplest system is a sign-up list with categories: one or two mains, two sides, a salad, bread, a dessert, drinks. Ask guests to claim a category rather than a dish, and let people cook what they cook best. If two people both want dessert, one can bring a fruit plate instead. And always ask about allergies and dietary needs in the invitation, not at the door.

body.heading: On the night
paragraphs: Put out name cards for dishes — "Maya's lentil soup (vegan)" — so guests with dietary needs can relax and browse instead of interrogating every plate. Keep the food flowing in the order people can actually eat it: set the table so guests move from mains to sides to dessert without a traffic jam.

The best part of a potluck is that it ends with sharing: recipes swapped, containers lent, leftovers packed up for someone's lunch tomorrow. Thank people by name for what they brought, and mean it — the dish was the gift, and noticing it is the thank-you.

description: A potluck works when the host thinks about the table, not the menu. A simple sign-up list, clear dish labels and a warm thank-you are all it takes.
